Title: Canadian Tourism Collapse — National
Description: Canadian visitor volume declined 26%+ Jan-Oct 2025 vs 2024. 11 consecutive months of YoY decline through Nov 2025. Land -30%, Air -24% in Oct.
Analysis: Most severe and sustained Canadian tourism decline on record. Structural shift, not seasonal variation.
Source: Statistics Canada; CBP via JEC Report
What to Track: Monthly Statistics Canada releases; signs of stabilization
Invalidation Criteria: Decline moderates to <10% for 3+ months

Title: Canadian Tourism — Regional Impacts
Description: Las Vegas -20%, Florida -16.9% Q1/-20% Q2, Fort Lauderdale hotels -32%, Buffalo cross-border -30%/shoppers -83%, Vermont spending -49%
Analysis: Geographic breadth validates national phenomenon. Spending declines exceed visitor count declines.
Source: LVCVA, Visit Florida, local reporting
What to Track: Regional economic indicators; business closure reports
Invalidation Criteria: Regional impacts stabilize despite national decline

Title: International Arrivals — Below Pre-Pandemic
Description: Dec 2025: 3.2M overseas visitors (8% below 2019). Full-year forecast: -6.3% to -8.2%. Recovery to pre-pandemic not expected until 2029.
Analysis: International inbound travel stalled. Multi-year structural challenge. US losing global tourism market share.
Source: NTTO/Commerce; US Travel Association
What to Track: Monthly NTTO releases; comparison to other destinations
Invalidation Criteria: Arrivals recover to within 5% of 2019

Title: International Arrivals — Regional Breakdown
Description: W. Europe volatile (-17% Mar, -5.5% Nov); Germany -11.6%; France -6.9%; Asia -25% vs 2019; Mexico +13.9% (bright spot)
Analysis: Regional variation suggests multiple causal factors. European decline improving but volatile. Asia deeply depressed. Mexico growth partially offsets.
Source: NTTO/Commerce
What to Track: NTTO by region; European booking trends; Asia recovery
Invalidation Criteria: Asia recovers to within 10% of 2019

Title: Florida Tourism Decline
Description: Canadian visitors: -16.9% Q1, -20% Q2. Fort Lauderdale hotels -32%. Florida is largest US tourism economy with outsized Canadian exposure.
Analysis: Q1→Q2 deterioration indicates worsening, not stabilizing. Critical for Florida triple exposure thesis.
Source: Visit Florida (quarterly)
What to Track: Q3 Visit Florida; winter snowbird bookings; FL hotel occupancy
Invalidation Criteria: Q3 shows improvement; winter bookings recover

Title: Tourism Economic Impact — Spending Loss
Description: Spending loss: $5.7-8.3B (US Travel); up to $30B (WTTC). Trade deficit ~$70B (was surplus). Per 1% drop = $1.8B lost.
Analysis: Spending impact exceeds visitor count decline. Trade balance reversal is significant macro shift.
Source: US Travel Association; Tourism Economics; WTTC
What to Track: Updated spending estimates; trade balance data
Invalidation Criteria: Spending stabilizes; trade balance improves

Description: DHS: 2.5M departures (605K deported + 1.9M self-deported). MPI: ~340K. Brookings: 310-315K. TRAC: 290,603. 65K detained (74% no criminal conviction).
Analysis: ⚠️ DATA QUALITY: DHS claims 7-8x higher than independent estimates. Weight independent sources higher. Self-deportation methodology disputed.
Source: DHS; MPI; Brookings; TRAC
What to Track: TRAC monthly; MPI analysis; DHS methodology clarification

Title: Agricultural Employment Collapse
Description: -155,000 workers Mar-Jul 2025 vs +2.2% same period 2024. 42% of farmworkers undocumented (~225K at risk).
Analysis: Most severe workforce displacement signal. Complete reversal from prior year. Peak season impact. Validates thesis strongly.
Source: BLS; Economic Insights report
What to Track: Monthly BLS; USDA Farm Labor; crop reports; food prices
Invalidation Criteria: Employment recovers; shortage doesn't affect supply/prices

Title: Construction Employment Divergence
Description: High-immigrant states (CA,TX,FL,AZ): -0.1%. Other states: +1.9%. 2pp divergence. 25% of construction undocumented (~1.5M at risk).
Analysis: Divergence is the key signal. National growing but immigrant-heavy states flat/negative. Approaching CRITICAL threshold.
Source: BLS State Employment; Economic Insights
What to Track: Monthly BLS state data; divergence widening or narrowing
Invalidation Criteria: Divergence narrows; high-immigrant states catch up

Title: Net Migration Turned Negative
Description: CBO: -290K to -525K net migration for 2025 (historic negative). Penn Wharton: 4yr 10%/yr removal → -1% GDP, +$350B deficit.
Analysis: Historically unprecedented. First negative net migration in modern era. Major structural shift for labor force and economy.
Source: CBO; Brookings; Penn Wharton
What to Track: CBO demographic updates; annual Census
Invalidation Criteria: Net migration returns positive >300K in 2026

Description: ~9M Americans abroad. UK passport apps: 1,900+ Q1 (record). Irish apps: 4,700 Q1 (decade high). CBO voluntary emigration: 430K. 53% political motivation.

Source: State Dept; UK Home Office; Ireland DFA; CBO

Description: FL property insurance: 4.5x national average, +72% since 2019. Multiple insurer exits. Citizens (state insurer) growing rapidly.
Analysis: Strongest LEADING indicator. Directly affects affordability and relocation decisions. Unavoidable cost. Mechanism is economic.
Source: Insurance industry data; state regulatory filings
What to Track: Annual rate filings; insurer activity; Citizens policy count
Invalidation Criteria: Insurance costs stabilize; new insurers enter; reforms reduce costs

Title: Sunbelt-Snowbelt Price Reversal
Description: FL metros: Miami -12.4%, Orlando -5.6%, Tampa -5.5%, Jacksonville -6.1%. Snowbelt: Wichita +21.2%, Toledo +16.4%, Buffalo +12.2%.
Analysis: Historic reversal of multi-decade pattern. 15-30pp differential. Leading indicator — precedes migration by 12-24 months.
Source: Zillow; Case-Shiller; Redfin

Description: MO, WI: net gains (first time in years). OH, MI, IL: declines slowing. CT: turnaround. Sunbelt still dominant (NC, FL, SC, TX, TN = 65% inbound).

Source: Harvard JCHS; MoveBuddha; Census

Description: SF Fed (Leduc & Wilson): "Snow Belt to Sun Belt migration likely to ultimately be reversed." First Street: 55M relocations by 2055, 5.2M in 2025.
Analysis: Academic/institutional validation. LONG-TERM thesis (5-15 years). Leading indicators firing now; migration follows with lag.
Source: SF Fed; First Street Foundation

Description: Q3 2025: 34.3M total visitors (+0.3% YoY). Canadian visitors: 507K (-15.1% YoY). Overseas: 2.3M (+3.2%). YTD Canadian: -15.5%. Q3 Canadian decline improved from Q2 (-20%) but still elevated.

Description: United Van Lines 2025 Study: Florida now "balanced" (52.2% inbound vs 47.8% outbound). FL dropped from high-inbound list (was on since 2018). Study notes "rising housing costs constraining traditionally attractive regions."
Analysis: SIGNIFICANT: Leading indicators (insurance 4.5x, price reversal) are transmitting to migration faster than expected 12-24mo lag. This validates FLOW-IMG-01 mechanism. VX-MARCO-3.03 should upgrade to ELEVATED.

Description: Statistics Canada Dec 2025: Return trips by air -18.7%, by automobile -30.7%. November: air -19.3%, auto -28.6%. Now 11-12 consecutive months of YoY decline.
Analysis: Decline sustained through full 2025. No reversal signals. Pattern consistent with structural shift, not temporary disruption. Competing hypothesis "Temporary Disruption" weakening.
Source: Statistics Canada Leading Indicator releases (Dec 10, Jan 12)
What to Track: Jan-Feb 2026 data; any signs of stabilization
Invalidation Criteria: Decline moderates to <10% for 3+ months

Title: U-Haul 2025: Florida #2 — Diverges from UVL
Description: U-Haul 2025 Growth Index (Jan 5, 2026): Florida ranks #2 (climbed from #4 in 2024). 50.6% inbound vs 49.4% outbound. Arrivals +2% YoY, departures +1% YoY. Texas #1. 8 of top 10 growth CITIES are in Florida (Ocala #1).
Analysis: METHODOLOGICAL DIVERGENCE: U-Haul shows FL #2 growth state (improved), while UVL shows FL "balanced" (dropped from high-inbound). Both sources show ~50-52% inbound — similar percentages, different interpretation. UVL uses 55% threshold for "high-inbound"; U-Haul ranks by net gain where even slim positive margin = growth. Convergent finding: Florida is no longer a strong inbound magnet but still net positive. DIY movers (U-Haul) may differ from full-service (UVL) customers.
Source: U-Haul Growth Index 2025 (Jan 5, 2026)
What to Track: Future years U-Haul vs UVL comparison; city vs state trends
Invalidation Criteria: U-Haul and UVL converge on same interpretation

Analysis: SHORTAGE SIGNAL CONFIRMED: Wage premium in agricultural sector validates labor scarcity from VX-MARCO-2.02 (-155K workers). Employers bidding up wages to compete for scarce labor. Supports workforce displacement thesis.
Source: USDA Farm Labor Survey; Farm Bureau AEWR analysis; BLS

Invalidation Criteria: Wage premium narrows; domestic workers fill gap at lower wages

Description: FL/TX/AZ construction wages below national average (~$42K vs $44K) BUT wage GROWTH >2x national rate (3.6%). Labor shortage driving rapid wage increases despite lower base.

Source: BLS FRED; ZipRecruiter; CareerSource Central Florida

Description: Mexico remittances down ~5% Jan-Nov 2025 vs 2024 ($56B vs $60B). June 2025: -16.2% YoY (steepest since 2012). 8 consecutive months of decline. First annual decline in >10 years. CONTRAST: Central America UP (Honduras +24%, Guatemala +19.5%, El Salvador +16.3%).

Title: Florida Housing Inventory — Condo Market Distress
Description: FL single-family: 4.6 months supply (Dec 2025). FL condo-townhouse: 8.8 months supply. Miami single-family: 6.6 months. Charlotte County: 6.9 months. National avg: 4.6 months.
Analysis: SPLIT MARKET: Single-family near balanced (4.6 mo), but condo market approaching distress (8.8 mo near BREACHED threshold of 9+). Condo segment has highest exposure to: (1) investor/second-home buyers affected by insurance; (2) Canadian snowbirds; (3) speculative purchases. Validates targeted stress in vulnerable segments.
Source: Florida Realtors; Redfin; Miami Realtors
What to Track: Monthly Florida Realtors data; condo vs single-family divergence; regional variation
Invalidation Criteria: Condo inventory declines below 6 months; market re-balances

Title: Florida Days on Market Extended — Buyer's Market Confirmed
Description: FL median DOM: 80 days (Dec 2025), 98 days (Nov 2025). +41% YoY from March 2024 baseline (53 days → 75 days). US median: 77 days. Naples: 140 days. Fort Lauderdale: 112 days. West Palm: 105 days. Industry standard: >70 days = buyer's market.
Analysis: BUYER'S MARKET CONFIRMED: Statewide DOM exceeds 70-day threshold. Luxury markets (Naples 140d, FLL 112d, WPB 105d) showing severe extension. +41% YoY increase is significant velocity decline. Combined with inventory data (ML-IMG-08), confirms FL real estate market stress beyond price metrics alone.
Source: Florida Realtors; Redfin; HousingWire; Houzeo
What to Track: Monthly DOM trends; luxury vs affordable segment comparison; seasonal patterns
Invalidation Criteria: DOM declines below 60 days; market velocity recovers

Title: Canadian Tourism Decline — Driver Attribution Analysis
Description: DRIVER MODEL: Political sentiment/boycott (55-65%), Exchange rate (15-20%), Alternative destination habits (10-15%), Economic conditions (5-10%), Travel friction (5%). KEY EVIDENCE: 91% want less US reliance; 68% think less of US; 63% less likely to visit due to politics; cross-partisan boycott participation. SUBSTITUTION PROOF: Mexico +11.8% (1.94M), France +49%, Portugal +40%, Cuba +17%, Air Canada launched 11 new non-US routes. Canadians ARE traveling, just not to US.
Analysis: 🔑 CRITICAL FINDING: Decline is PRIMARILY POLITICAL, not economic. If economic (exchange rate, budget), we'd see overall travel decline. Instead we see SUBSTITUTION — Canadians traveling MORE to alternatives while avoiding US. This is behavioral, not financial. Implications: (1) Reversal requires political change, not economic recovery; (2) Habit formation in alternatives may cause permanent share loss; (3) "Temporary Disruption" hypothesis significantly weakened.
Source: Wikipedia 2025 Canadian boycott; CBC; Nanos Research; CTV; Statistics Canada; Mexico News Daily; Travel and Tour World
What to Track: Quarterly sentiment surveys; alternative destination growth; boycott duration surveys
Invalidation Criteria: Political de-escalation; sentiment surveys show >50% willing to return

Title: Canadian Boycott Duration Survey Data
Description: Nanos Research: 47% say boycott ends only after Trump leaves (post-Jan 2029); 28% say ends during Trump term; 16% say PERMANENT; 9% unsure. DEMOGRAPHIC SPLITS: Age 55+ (snowbirds): 22% believe permanent. Age 18-34: only 9% permanent. Regional: Quebec/Atlantic more likely permanent; Alberta most likely to return (31% planning US trips 2026).
Analysis: REVERSAL PROBABILITY LOW: Only 28% expect boycott to end by mid-2026. Invalidation criterion "rebounds to within 10% of 2024 by mid-2026" has ~10-15% probability of firing. Key demographic: 55+ age group (snowbirds) has HIGHEST permanent boycott belief (22%) — this is the exact population FL depends on.
Source: Nanos Research via CTV; Longwoods International; Blue Cross Travel Study
What to Track: Quarterly boycott duration surveys; Alberta travel intentions; snowbird booking data
Invalidation Criteria: Survey shows >40% expecting near-term return; Alberta leads recovery

Title: Canadian Alternative Destination Growth — Habit Formation Risk
Description: Mexico: 1.94M Canadian visitors 2025 (+11.8%). France: +49.1% Q2. Portugal: +40% (now #1 EU destination). Cuba: +17%. Jamaica: 289K. Air Canada: 11 new routes to Mexico/Caribbean/South America (largest-ever non-US expansion). WestJet: -25% US demand, scaling back US routes.
Analysis: ⚠️ STRUCTURAL RISK: Airlines investing in non-US capacity creates infrastructure lock-in. Once Canadian snowbirds discover Mexico/Caribbean alternatives with comparable weather and lower costs, habit formation may cause PERMANENT market share loss even if political tensions ease. This is not priced into "Temporary Disruption" hypothesis.
Source: Mexico News Daily; Travel and Tour World; Air Canada; WestJet
What to Track: Air Canada/WestJet route announcements; Mexico/Caribbean Canadian visitor trends; snowbird destination surveys
Invalidation Criteria: Canadian travel to alternatives declines; airlines restore US capacity

Title: Texas Housing Market Distress — Approaching 2007-08 Levels
Description: TX statewide inventory 5.5 months (Sep 2025). Austin: 31 consecutive months YoY price decline; median $435K (-3.3% Dec). Houston $371K, Dallas $440K, San Antonio $335K — all declining. 53.4% Austin listings with price cuts. New listings at record pace; inventory growth nearly 2x rate of Great Financial Crisis build-up.
Analysis: 🔑 SECOND-STRONGEST HOUSING SIGNAL after Florida. Austin pattern (31 consecutive months) is longer than FL decline. Inventory approaching historic distress levels. Texas differs from FL: no insurance crisis, but workforce displacement + border economy stress compound. Watch for convergence with FL pattern.
Source: Texas Real Estate Research Center; Redfin; Norada Real Estate
What to Track: Monthly TRERC data; Austin price trajectory; inventory levels vs 2007-08
Invalidation Criteria: Austin prices stabilize; inventory declines below 4 months

Title: Texas Workforce Displacement — Highest Enforcement Concentration
Description: Texas = 1/4 of ALL US ICE arrests (138K nationwide through Jul, ~35K in TX). 37-40% construction workforce foreign-born. Dallas Fed: job growth 1.2% (lowest since pandemic), citing immigration crackdown. 40% of firms report workers missing shifts due to fear. One in five small businesses report lost employees.
Analysis: 🔑 TEXAS IS GROUND ZERO for workforce displacement. Concentration of enforcement creates amplified local effects. Construction sector most exposed — 1/3 workers foreign-born. Job growth slowdown validates economic transmission. Direct Fed attribution strengthens causal inference.
Source: Dallas Fed; Texas Tribune; Border Report; American Immigration Council
What to Track: Dallas Fed employment reports; ICE Texas data; construction project delays
Invalidation Criteria: TX job growth recovers to >2%; enforcement moderates

Title: Texas Border Economy Stress — Integrated Production Disrupted

Moody's: "local governments on US-Mexico border will begin to experience slowing economic activity and potential budgetary stress." El Paso: immigrants earned $4.8B (2019), $1B in taxes. Laredo: 53% of business owners are immigrant entrepreneurs.
Analysis: CROSS-BORDER INTEGRATION: Texas-Mexico economies "not separate for most practical purposes" (Texas A&M). Tariffs + immigration enforcement = dual shock to integrated supply chains. Border cities face revenue stress from declining Mexican cross-border shopping + workforce departures.
Source: Dallas Fed; Moody's; American Immigration Council; Texas A&M Mosbacher Institute
What to Track: Border city sales tax data; bridge toll revenue; Moody's municipal ratings
Invalidation Criteria: Border retail stabilizes; cross-border flows normalize

Title: California Wildfire Insurance Crisis — Structural Parallel to Florida
Description: Jan 2025 LA fires: $35-45B insured losses; 16K structures destroyed; 29+ deaths. FAIR Plan (state insurer of last resort) requesting +35% rate increase for spring 2026. 100K+ homeowner non-renewals since 2019. $800B-$1.3T coverage gap in high-risk areas. Premiums +20-30% combined filings. 4 in 10 policyholders report insurability issues.
Analysis: 🔑 STRUCTURAL PARALLEL TO FLORIDA: Both states face climate-driven insurance market dysfunction with state insurer of last resort growing rapidly. Key difference: FL crisis is diffuse (statewide hurricane), CA crisis is geographic (wildfire zones). CA implementing regulatory reforms (catastrophe modeling) FL has not. Watch for divergence or convergence in outcomes.
Source: CA DOI; McKinsey; CalMatters; KQED
What to Track: FAIR Plan policy count; rate filing approvals; non-renewal data; high-risk zone pricing
Invalidation Criteria: Insurers return to CA; non-renewals reverse; coverage gap narrows

Title: California Ag Workforce Disruption — Acute Enforcement Impact
Description: CA = nation's largest farm state. 9/10 crop workers foreign-born; 56% undocumented. Kern County: crews dropped from 30 to 5 workers ("hiding at home"). Ventura County: 25-45% attendance drop following June 2025 ICE intensification. Average farmworker age rising (up 7 years since 2006). 50% of farms operating with 20% workforce deficit.
Analysis: 🔑 CALIFORNIA AG IS CANARY: Highest undocumented workforce share (56%) means enforcement impact is most visible here. Immediate crop-level effects (unharvested fields) provide real-time validation of workforce departure thesis. Watch for food price transmission — if it appears anywhere, CA produce should show first.
Source: USDA; PPIC; Xinhua; Farmonaut; KCUR
What to Track: CA crop reports; harvest completion rates; CA produce prices vs national
Invalidation Criteria: Workforce attendance recovers; H-2A expansion fills gap

Description: Vegas tourism down 7.4% to decade-low (35.5M visitors through Nov, matching 2000-2003). 9 consecutive months decline. Canadian flights: Air Canada -33%, WestJet -31%, Flair -62%. Canadians = largest international visitor segment (1.5M in 2024); contributed $3.6B to Southern NV economy; supported 43K jobs. Unemployment 5.8% (3rd highest major metro).
Analysis: 🔑 SINGLE-VECTOR CONCENTRATION: Unlike FL (triple exposure), Vegas faces Canadian tourism as PRIMARY stress vector. No workforce or insurance compounding. But concentration creates severe local impact — 43K jobs dependent on Canadian visitors. Mayor making direct appeals ("We love you, we need you, we miss you"). Tests whether single-vector stress can reach economic significance.
Source: LVCVA; CBC; Fortune; Fox News; Statistics Canada
What to Track: Monthly LVCVA data; Canadian airline capacity; Vegas unemployment
Invalidation Criteria: Canadian flights stabilize; Vegas tourism recovers to >-5% YoY

Title: Austin Housing Correction — Root Cause Analysis (Session 7 Deep-Dive)
Description: Austin experienced +72.5% price surge Mar 2020-Jun 2022, making it most overvalued US metro (63.7% per Moody's Q1 2022). Median jumped $369K→$625K in 2 years. Drivers: remote work revolution, record-low rates (2.5-3%), tech relocations (Tesla, Oracle, Google, Apple, Meta), no state income tax, #1 domestic migration destination. TRIPLE SHOCK ended boom mid-2022: (1) Fed rate hikes 3%→7%+; (2) Return-to-office mandates; (3) Tech sector contraction (245K layoffs 2025). Speculative unwinding: institutional buyers dropped 29%→6.1%. Current: 31 months decline, median $435K (-18-26% from peak), 88 DOM (highest since 2011), 54.3% price cuts.
Analysis: 🔑 KEY FINDING: Austin correction is PANDEMIC OVERSHOOT UNWINDING, not same causal mechanism as Florida. FL driven by insurance/climate/tourism; Austin driven by tech/speculation/rate sensitivity. Pattern validates regional housing stress but through DIFFERENT transmission mechanism. Analysts expect bottom late 2026/early 2027. Parcl Labs bearish (-16.5% additional decline); consensus is correction not crash.
Source: TRERC; Redfin; Zillow; Moody's; Parcl Labs; KUT Radio; Spyglass Realty; Norada
What to Track: Austin price trajectory; tech hiring; institutional buyer return
Invalidation Criteria: Austin prices stabilize; tech hiring resumes; bottom confirmed

Title: Texas Border Economy — Acute Stress Signals (Session 7 Deep-Dive)
Description: RIO GRANDE VALLEY (Q1 2025): Conveyances -14.7% YoY, Travelers -14.6% YoY. Dallas Fed: "trade uncertainty weighing on businesses." CITY-LEVEL: Laredo -1.3% economic contraction; McAllen 6.1% unemployment (highest on border); El Paso monitoring "potential financial downturn from tariffs, layoffs." STRUCTURAL SHIFT: Mexican shopper retail share declined from 40%+ to 15-28% over two decades as Mexican big-box stores expanded. Visa costs up ($185→$435). Only 5% of crossers cite exchange rate; 53% cite wait times. TARIFF EXPOSURE: 100K jobs at risk in El Paso-Juárez corridor; USMCA review July 2026 creates major uncertainty. MANUFACTURING: Mexico auto production -0.9% to 3.95M units; 10K job losses. Nonprofit sector collapse: Southwest Key 1,200-1,300 layoffs.
Analysis: 🔑 DUAL STRESS: Border economy faces (1) STRUCTURAL long-term decline in cross-border shopping dependency AND (2) ACUTE 2025 stress from enforcement/tariffs/uncertainty. Unlike FL's tourism shock, border stress is BILATERAL — affects both US cities and integrated Mexican production. USMCA July 2026 review is critical inflection point. Moody's warning on municipal finances validates fiscal transmission risk.
Source: Dallas Fed; TRERC; Moody's; Texas Tribune; FreightWaves; Tax Foundation
What to Track: Border city sales tax; bridge toll revenue; USMCA review outcome
Invalidation Criteria: Cross-border flows normalize; USMCA renewed without disruption

Analysis: 🔑 BREAKTHROUGH: Dallas Fed provides DIRECT ATTRIBUTION of Texas employment weakness to immigration enforcement. This is the clearest institutional validation of the workforce displacement thesis. Torres quote: "Higher productivity is suppressing labor demand, and less immigration is constraining labor supply." Texas is GROUND ZERO for enforcement impact (1/4 of all arrests) but also has most robust data from Dallas Fed research.

Title: Texas vs Florida Pattern Comparison (Session 7 Synthesis)
Description: HOUSING: Austin correction DEEPER (-18-26% from peak) and LONGER (31 months) than any FL metro. But different cause: Austin = pandemic speculation unwinding; FL = insurance/climate push. TX statewide inventory (5.5mo) similar to FL SF (4.6mo); TX lacks FL condo distress (8.8mo). WORKFORCE: TX has MORE CONCENTRATED enforcement impact (24% of all ICE arrests vs FL's diffuse exposure). Dallas Fed provides direct attribution FL lacks. TOURISM: FL has Canadian tourism crisis (BREACHED -26%); TX has border retail decline (structural 40%→15-28% + acute -14.7% traffic). Different mechanisms but similar outcome (revenue loss). INSURANCE: FL has crisis (4.5x national, BREACHED); TX has NO insurance crisis. This is KEY DIFFERENCE. CLASSIFICATION: FL = TRIPLE EXPOSURE (tourism + workforce + insurance); TX = DUAL EXPOSURE (workforce + housing) with unique border vector.
Analysis: 🔑 SYNTHESIS: Texas validates MULTI-STATE pattern but through DIFFERENT transmission mechanisms. Key insight: housing stress can emerge from multiple causes (pandemic speculation, insurance push, workforce shortage). The COMMON THREAD is that traditional indicators miss or lag these effects. Texas strengthens thesis by showing pattern is not FL-specific while also revealing limits of direct comparison. FL's triple exposure remains more severe; TX's dual exposure is more concentrated in specific vectors.
Source: Session 7 synthesis of ML-TX-01 through ML-TX-06, ML-IMG-01 through ML-IMG-09

Title: Florida Net Domestic Migration Collapse — Census 2024
Description: Census Bureau 2024: FL net domestic migration fell from +317,923 (2022) to +185,067 (2023) to +63,346 (2024) — an 80% collapse in two years. International migration (+411,322) now drives FL population growth. Total population still growing (+467,347 or 2.0%) due to international inflows masking domestic outflow deceleration.
Analysis: 🔑 STRONGEST OFFICIAL VALIDATION: Leading indicators (insurance 4.5x, housing reversal) are transmitting to migration FASTER than expected 12-24 month lag. 80% collapse in two years is unprecedented for a top destination state. Validates VX-MARCO-3.03 upgrade to ELEVATED and supports UVL "balanced" finding. International migration is now the primary driver of FL population growth.
Source: Census Bureau Population Estimates; Redfin analysis
What to Track: Census 2025 release (~Dec 2026); continuation of decline trajectory
Invalidation Criteria: Domestic migration recovers to >150K; international migration slows

Title: IRS SOI Migration Data — Pre-Shift Baseline (2021-2022)
Description: IRS tax filer data (2021-2022, most recent available): FL +261,863 net individuals (+126,837 returns). TX +182,704 net (+83,136 returns). CA -355,809 (largest outflow). NY -267,156. NY→FL was second largest migration corridor (91K/year). Demographics: FL attracted older migrants (55+); TX attracted younger (60.4% ages 26-45). FL AGI gains among highest nationally.
Analysis: BASELINE REFERENCE: Establishes pre-shift migration patterns when FL was still dominant destination. IRS data has 18-24 month lag, so 2023-2024 collapse not yet captured. When 2022-2023 data releases (~late 2026), watch for FL decline. Age demographics explain why FL vulnerable to insurance costs (older homeowners) while TX vulnerable to workforce disruption (younger workers).
Source: IRS SOI Tax Stats; Tax Foundation analysis
What to Track: IRS 2022-2023 data release (~late 2026)
Invalidation Criteria: FL net migration in IRS data declines >30% from 2021-22 baseline

Title: Florida School Enrollment Decline — Family Outmigration Signal
Description: Miami-Dade County lost 13,059 students in first 9 days of 2024-25 school year vs prior year (326K→313K). Statewide decline of 12,379 projected (2.366M→2.354M, -0.5%). State forecasters: FL schools will not return to pre-pandemic enrollment in next decade. Miami-Dade Superintendent Dotres attributes to: (1) lower birth rates, (2) families leaving South Florida, (3) fewer immigrants entering. Pinellas County -3,651 (77.8K→74.2K).
Analysis: INDEPENDENT VALIDATION: School enrollment is less confounded than moving company data — families with children are "stickier" and don't move casually. Superintendent explicitly citing "families leaving South Florida" is notable official attribution. -100K students projected vs pre-pandemic by 2034-35. Confounding factors: 13% of FL students now in private voucher programs (highest in nation); birth rate decline is real.
Source: Florida DOE; Miami-Dade Schools; The 74; Florida Phoenix
What to Track: FL DOE enrollment reports; 2025-26 school year data
Invalidation Criteria: Enrollment stabilizes; superintendent stops citing departure as cause

Title: Florida International Migration Pipeline Collapse
Description: TRIPLE CHOKEPOINT: (1) CHNV parole terminated Mar 2025 — 532K lost status, ~80% in South FL (110K Cubans, 211K Haitians, 93K Nicaraguans, 117K Venezuelans). (2) TPS Venezuela cancelled Oct 2025 — 350K+ affected, FL has 404K TPS holders total (largest state). (3) Darién Gap closed 99% — crossings fell from 302K (2024) to 3K (2025). Miami-Dade had +124K international migration in 2024 (highest US county) which offset -67K domestic outflow. Pipeline now severed at source AND existing population losing status/work authorization.
Analysis: 🔑 THESIS ACCELERANT: International migration was masking Florida's domestic outflow collapse. This mask is dissolving. The 411K international migrants that drove FL population growth in 2024 are unsustainable: (1) pipeline closed, (2) legal pathways terminated, (3) existing residents face deportation. Venezuelan/Haitian immigrants = majority of recent FL arrivals, both groups lost status. 95% of TPS holders were employed — now lose work authorization. FL may face POPULATION CLIFF in 2026-27 if both domestic AND international turn negative. Labor market shock compounds tourism/construction stress.
Source: DHS; USCIS; Census Bureau; Migration Policy Institute; NBC Miami; CiberCuba
What to Track: Census 2025 international migration data; USCIS deportation stats; TPS termination effects
Invalidation Criteria: International migration recovers to >200K; new legal pathways created

Title: Florida Immigrant Workforce Loss — Dual Labor Supply Shock
Description: FL immigrant workforce share: Agriculture 47%, Construction 38%, Hospitality 25%. CHNV/TPS termination removes work authorization for 500K+ workers in FL. Current shortages: 500K+ job vacancies statewide; 439K construction workers needed; Miami-Dade schools were filling positions with Venezuelan/Haitian arrivals. 18% of Venezuelan immigrants in poverty; 60% of FL renters cost-burdened. Hospitality lobby requested "Essential Worker Act" to create permits; construction industry wants H-2C visas. Florida businesses NEED immigrant labor but policy removing workers while domestic migration slowing.
Analysis: DUAL SHOCK: (1) Domestic workers leaving due to insurance/affordability (MARCO thesis), AND (2) immigrant workers losing legal status simultaneously. This creates labor shortage that cannot be filled by either source. Paradox: FL has 500K vacancies but removing workers who fill them. Industries most affected (construction, hospitality, agriculture) are also most exposed to tourism decline and housing stress. Wage pressure upward but employers can't afford higher wages due to demand destruction. Potential for economic contraction if labor shortage + demand weakness combine.
Source: FL Policy Institute; American Immigration Council; Orlando Sentinel; Sun-Sentinel; Associated General Contractors
What to Track: BLS FL employment by sector; job vacancy data; wage growth by industry
Invalidation Criteria: Labor shortage eases via legal visa expansion; or demand destruction reduces need for workers
